question: A 14-month-old girl is referred for weight-for-age below −2 SD. She is exclusively formula-fed; her mother is withdrawn and rarely makes eye contact during the consultation. Physical examination reveals no dysmorphic features, no hepatosplenomegaly, and normal thyroid. Which of the following best describes the most likely primary aetiology in this child?

answers.text: Organic — congenital hypothyroidism causing reduced caloric utilisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypothyroidism is an organic cause of FTT, but the normal examination (no goitre, no coarse features) and the prominent maternal withdrawal strongly favour a non-organic explanation.

answers.text: Non-organic — inadequate caloric intake driven by dysfunctional caregiver-infant interaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Maternal depression and dysfunctional feeding interactions are the most frequently missed non-organic causes of FTT. The absence of organic findings and the clinical picture of a withdrawn mother point directly here.

answers.text: Organic — cystic fibrosis causing malabsorption and increased caloric loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CF causes steatorrhoea and recurrent chest infections. The absence of respiratory symptoms and loose oily stools makes this unlikely in this presentation.

answers.text: Mixed — iron-deficiency anaemia combined with coeliac disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mixed causes exist, the clinical picture here is dominated by caregiver-related factors rather than evidence of malabsorption or micronutrient deficiency warranting this label.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the non-organic vs organic classification of FTT aetiology. A withdrawn, depressed caregiver is a sentinel finding that shifts probability strongly toward non-organic causes before any investigation is ordered.
Well done. Non-organic FTT — especially caregiver-infant interaction difficulties secondary to maternal depression — is the single most under-recognised aetiology in outpatient practice.
